To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1. Attention is slower to disengage from an object when the object’s features change slowly in time.
Temporal autocorrelation of visual stimuli increases the latency of attentional sampling.
the latency of visual selection is delayed when the feature changes gradually in time, relative to when the feature is changing abruptly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how attention samples information from a visual scene and the role that temporal autocorrelations play in that process.
the dynamics of attentional selection, and how the time course of selection depends on the nature of the information that is changing in time.
the question of how the brain deals with temporally correlated stimuli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the smoothness of a stimulus feature after the cue is presented increases selection latency.
temporal autocorrelations of a feature increase the latency at which the information is sampled.
attention is delayed by the smoothness of a feature, which is not the same as the smoothness of motion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
temporal autocorrelated features increase the time required to sample information from the visual scene.
attention is delayed when a visual feature changes gradually in time, but not when a feature changes rapidly.
the brain is more efficient at sampling temporally random visual information than temporally autocorrelating information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the latency of attention is not a fixed property of attentional selection.
attention is not only delayed when stimuli change abruptly, but also when they change gradually.
the latency of information selection can be influenced by the temporal autocorrelation structure of the stimulus.
